stops.name: Downieville Museum
stops.invite: A gold rush store built of flat stones in 1852, which survived fires that took most of the town.
story: The museum building dates to 1852, making it one of Downieville's first buildings. It was first used as a Chinese store, was known as the Old Slate Store, and later became the J.M.B. Meroux Building.

Its walls are made entirely of flat rocks laid horizontally, and the stone helped it survive fires that destroyed most of the town. The Meroux family gave the building to the community, and it has operated as a museum since 1932.

The core collection came from relics gathered by former Sheriff George C. Bynon. An older newspaper article describes exhibits such as ledgers, an 1874 map of Sierra County, gold scales and old firefighting gear.

facts.t: The building dates to 1852 and was first used as a Chinese store, later called the Old Slate Store.
Its walls are made of flat rocks laid horizontally, and the stone helped it survive fires that destroyed most of the town.
The Meroux family gave the building to the community, and it has been a museum since 1932.
The core collection is relics gathered by former Sheriff George C. Bynon.
A 1970 article, reprinted in 2023, lists ledgers, an 1874 map of Sierra County, a gold scale and old fire hoses among its exhibits.

stops.access: The museum is on Main Street in Downieville. A 1970 article gave seasonal hours, which may have changed, so check with the museum or Sierra County before you go. It is not confirmed to be open year-round.

access_check.how: Story read against NoeHill and a Mountain Messenger article reprinted in 2023 (the 1970 hours were not used). No current hours found. Not walked yet.

stops.name: Josefa Segovia Marker
stops.sens: This stop is about a lynching. It is told briefly and factually. You can skip any part.
stops.invite: A 2024 marker on Main Street remembers a woman hanged by a mob in 1851.
story: On July 5, 1851, a mob of Anglo-American miners hanged Josefa Segovia from the Jersey Bridge in Downieville after a mock trial. She was a Mexican-Californian woman, probably in her early to mid twenties, accused of stabbing a miner named Frederick Cannon.

Accounts differ about what happened the day before and on the day itself, and some modern writers doubt that she was the person who killed Cannon. Her name is also debated: she appears as Josefa Segovia, Juanita and Josefa Loaiza. She is described as the only known woman lynched in California, though the record is incomplete.

The marker was dedicated on August 24, 2024, by two chapters of E Clampus Vitus, a historical fraternal society. It is listed on Main Street in front of 326 Main Street, in the Downieville historic riverfront district.

facts.t: A mob hanged Josefa Segovia from the Jersey Bridge in Downieville on July 5, 1851, after a mock trial.
She was accused of stabbing a miner named Frederick Cannon; some modern commentators doubt she was the one who killed him.
Her name is debated, and she appears as Josefa Segovia, Juanita and Josefa Loaiza.
The marker was dedicated on August 24, 2024, by two E Clampus Vitus chapters.

stops.access: The marker is outdoors on Main Street, east of Commercial Street, and was listed as in front of the restaurant at 326 Main Street. Business names can change, so go by the street number. It is on a public street.

access_check.how: Marker listing and Wikipedia article read; the marker's wording was summarized, not copied. Not walked yet.

stops.name: Plumas-Eureka State Park
stops.invite: A mining camp park with stamp mills and a miner's bunkhouse museum, in the mountains of Plumas County.
story: The park is about five miles west of Blairsden on County Road A-14. It interprets the Gold Rush mining era, and the state landmark text here mentions Jamison City, which produced a famous 52-pound nugget, and the Eureka Mill and mine, which yielded $17 million.

The same landmark text calls Johnsville, then Johnstown, a well preserved town from 1849. The historic area has a museum in the miner's bunkhouse, the Mohawk Stamp Mill, the Bushman five-stamp mill, stables, a blacksmith shop and a mine office.
Eureka Peak, once called Gold Mountain, was the site of some of the first organized ski races in North America. The park is open to the public except during the winter season.

facts.t: The park is about five miles west of Blairsden on County Road A-14, in Plumas County.
California Historical Landmark No. 196 mentions Jamison City and its 52-pound nugget, and the Eureka Mill and mine yielding $17 million.
The historic area has a museum in the miner's bunkhouse, the Mohawk Stamp Mill and the Bushman five-stamp mill.
Eureka Peak, formerly Gold Mountain, hosted some of the first organized ski races in North America.
The park is open to the public except during the winter season.

stops.access: The park is on County Road A-14 in Plumas County and is open except during the winter season, when snow can limit access. Check California State Parks for current hours, fees and which buildings are open before you drive up.

access_check.how: Story read against Wikipedia and NoeHill's landmark text; current hours were not confirmed. Not walked yet.

stops.name: Beckwourth Pass
stops.invite: The lowest pass in the Sierra Nevada, found by a mountain man who turned it into a wagon road.
story: Beckwourth Pass sits at 5,221 feet at the northeastern edge of Sierra Valley, near the Plumas and Lassen County line. It is about 20 miles east of Portola and 25 miles northwest of Reno.

James Beckwourth is credited with finding it, in 1850 by Wikipedia and the National Park Service, and in 1851 by the state marker. In 1851 he improved the route into the Beckwourth Trail, which ran from Truckee Meadows (now Sparks, Nevada) through the pass and on to Marysville.

About 1,200 emigrants used the trail between 1851 and 1854, until it became a toll road. A narrow-gauge railroad used the pass from 1895 to 1916, and the Western Pacific Railroad built the 6,002-foot Chilcoot Tunnel under it in 1906. The Native Daughters of the Golden West placed a plaque here in 1937, and it is California Historical Landmark No. 336.

facts.t: The pass is 5,221 feet high, near the Plumas and Lassen County line, about 25 miles northwest of Reno.
James Beckwourth is credited with discovering it; the date is given as 1850 by Wikipedia and 1851 on the state marker.
The Beckwourth Trail ran from Truckee Meadows (now Sparks) through the pass to Marysville, and about 1,200 emigrants used it between 1851 and 1854.
The Western Pacific Railroad built the 6,002-foot Chilcoot Tunnel under the pass in 1906.
The marker was placed in 1937 by the Native Daughters of the Golden West, and the site is California Historical Landmark No. 336.

stops.access: The marker is beside State Route 70 near Chilcoot, a highway pull-off, so take care with traffic and park only where it is safe. Check road conditions in winter. The exact marker spot was not checked.

access_check.how: Story read against Wikipedia and NoeHill's landmark page; the pass coordinates come from Wikipedia and the marker position was not checked. Not walked yet.

stops.name: Jim Beckwourth Cabin Museum
stops.invite: A log cabin museum at the third trading post a mountain man built in Sierra Valley.
story: James Beckwourth built three successive trading posts in the northwest corner of Sierra Valley. The first two burned, and the log cabin here is the third, built after the second fire when trail traffic had declined. He likely had men build it from green logs, and he lived in it for about a year.

Beckwourth was born in 1798 in Virginia into slavery and was freed by his father in the 1820s. He trapped for the Rocky Mountain Fur Company and lived with a Crow band for years. How he came to join the Crow is disputed, and his autobiography, dictated in the winter of 1854 to 1855 and published in 1856, was doubted from the start.
He left California in November 1858 and went on to Denver, and he never returned. Plumas County owns the site, which is a museum run by a curator and docents.

facts.t: Beckwourth built three trading posts in Sierra Valley; the first two burned, and the log cabin is the third.
He dictated his autobiography in the winter of 1854 to 1855, and it was published in 1856.
He left for Missouri in November 1858, reached Denver in November 1859 and never returned to California.
He was born in Virginia in 1798 (some sources say 1800) into slavery, and his father freed him through deeds in 1824, 1825 and 1826.
How Beckwourth came to live with the Crow is contested, and reviewers doubted the accuracy of his autobiography from the start.
Plumas County owns the museum, which is open inside only on summer weekends, with signs outdoors the rest of the year.

stops.access: The grounds can be visited year-round with signs outside. The inside is open only on summer weekends, noon to 4 p.m., according to the National Park Service. Confirm before you drive out. The map point is a rough estimate of the town, so use the street address.

access_check.how: Story read against the National Park Service place page and Wikipedia's James Beckwourth article. Map point is the town of Beckwourth and is only a rough estimate. No free photo found. Not walked yet.
